And the lower court correctly ruled that at the time of the decedent's death, ROV was the legal child of the decedent. This ruling was not appealed. However, the court went on to say that in regards to this policy that's before this court, ROV would not be considered the child of the decedent. Making this determination, the court construed the policy and interpreted the policy and made errors in two different ways. First, there was the introduction of parole evidence. And second, it was redefining the term children. In regard to the introduction of parole evidence, there was no argument by appellees in the lower court nor is there a finding by the trial court that there was any language in the policy that the terms were ambiguous. And if you look at the policy that was included within the record and the sections that were cited by Appellant in our briefs, it's clear that the language is clear and unambiguous. The policy prescribes the benefits that are going to be paid out if a decedent did not leave a beneficiary, did not name a beneficiary. The first is a spouse. It's clear and undisputed that he did not have a spouse at the time of his death. The second is a child. There is no finding, nor can there really be that there is a latent defect in regards to the term children. Despite this fact, the court entered two documents to ostensibly help it define the term children for this policy. It entered a joint stipulation and a consent that were drafted and executed months before the decedent passed away. This joint stipulation and consent were executed to sever, were in agreement for a step-parent adoption to sever the rights of the decedent. Despite the fact that there was no ambiguity in the policy, the court used this joint stipulation and the consent to construe the policy to believe that the decedent did not believe that the ROB was his child at the time of his death. Not only does this violate public policy, but it creates an absurd result. It violates public policy in the sense that the courts have repeatedly ruled that any agreement to terminate the parent-child relationship without it relying upon a chapter 39 or an adoption is void. So parents cannot just come together and agree to terminate the rights of their children. It has to be pursuant to those proceedings. So if the court determines that this joint stipulation upon the decedent's execution of the document or he believed that it terminated his rights, violates the public policy and the joint stipulation there becomes void. And this undermines the entire purpose of that contract. This also creates an absurd result for the contract because the court, as I said in the beginning, the court found that ROB was the legal child for the decedent. He made this explicitly clear in his ruling. So the court in making this ruling was stating that the child was the child for the decedent for all purposes, except for this contract. That it doesn't make really very much sense at all and really creates a huge policy concern for these insurance contracts. So that there's going to be and could be litigation in regards to now who is a child. And if parents and children then become alienated, say adult parents or adult children or parents become alienated, then we have to come into as the subjective beliefs of parties in regards to whether or not they believed that was their parent or child at the time of their death. It just, it creates a huge problem.
